title: Ramanand: where shall I go
hookLine: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love (Basant, Ramanand, ang 1195)

cards: The bag is packed. The offering is ready: sandalwood, ground fine, mixed with sweet oils, the good stuff saved for a holy day. You're at the door, keys in hand, about to set out for the temple.
And then you stop, set the bag down, and don't go. Not out of laziness. Because something just became clear.
That's where Ramanand's hymn begins: at the door.

teach.h: WHERE SHALL I GO? MY HOME IS COLORED.
teach.b: Three days ago, Sain the barber named a teacher: Ramanand, who knows the devotion of the Lord. Today Ramanand speaks for himself, in Raag Basant, the raag of spring, on Ang 1195.
It opens with a question, in paraphrase: where shall I go? My own home is colored with love. My mind no longer wanders off; it has gone still.
Then he tells how. One day a longing rose up in me. I ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship God at the holy place.
And the Guru showed me that God within my own mind.

teach.h: SANDALWOOD READY, THE TRIP TURNS AROUND.
teach.b: The trip turned around at the door. Next, a line with a gentle sting. Wherever I go, I find water and stone: bathing places and carved images.
But You fill them all, equally. I've looked through the Vedas and the Puranas, the old scriptures.

teach.h: GO THERE ONLY IF HE ISN'T HERE.
teach.b: Go there, he says, only if He isn't here. He doesn't say the temple is empty or the old books worthless.
He says the One who fills the temple fills the home too, and everything equally, so the long walk isn't needed to find what's already here.
The close, in paraphrase: True Guru, I'm a sacrifice to You, who cut away all my confusion and doubt.

teach.h: THE GURU'S WORD CUTS THE DOUBT.
teach.b: Ramanand's Lord is the all-pervading One, and the Guru's Word cuts away countless deeds. Tradition remembers Ramanand as a teacher whose circle reached far, and some say Kabir learned from him.
In the Granth, he leaves one image: a house dyed with love, so full there's nowhere else to go.

how: Ramanand's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Basant, and Sikh teaching speaks of finding the Lord within, guided by the Guru's Word.

o: a teacher who found God at home, not on a trip
a pilgrim who walked to every holy river
a king who built a temple of sandalwood

p: my own home is colored with love

s: Ramanand never set out for the temple
he did: he ground sandalwood and set out, and the Guru showed him God within his own mind.
Ramanand says the old scriptures are worthless
he says he looked through the Vedas and Puranas, and that you go there only if He isn't here.
Sain names Ramanand in his own hymn
Ramanand knows the devotion of the Lord, Sain sings.

games.q: you're Ramanand, sandalwood ground and oils mixed, ready to set out to worship at the holy place. what happens?
o: you go, and find God waiting there.
the Guru shows you God within your own mind.
you give the sandalwood away and stay angry.
games.why: the Guru showed me that God within my own mind, he sings, and then asks: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love?

practice: Stay right where you are, in whatever room this is, and don't wish yourself somewhere holier: notice the wall, the light, the sounds from the next room or the street.
If the mind wants to pack a bag and go somewhere better, let it set the bag down. If you pray, say Waheguru on the breath out; if you don't, simply stay.

wordCard.voice: Ramanand. The teacher Sain named, whose hymn in Raag Basant turns around at the door: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: color, dye, love; Ramanand's home is 'colored' with it (Ang 1195).

carryVoice: Your line: colored at home. The room you're in counts, just as it is. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Basant, Ramanand (kat jaaeeai re ghar laago rang), Ang 1195
